claims.text: The proposed repair targets damaged high-value components made from advanced titanium alloys or high-entropy alloys.
The target alloys have microstructures that are sensitive to fusion-induced defects and hot cracking.
Optimized UAM with real-time monitoring can produce a high-integrity solid-state repair overlay.
A UAM repair overlay can match or exceed the parent material's performance under aggressive operating conditions.
UAM eliminates the hot-cracking risk attributed to fusion-welding repair.
UAM deposits the repair overlay layer by layer from thin metallic foils.
Ultrasonic vibration induces mechanical consolidation and atomic interdiffusion without melting.
Optimizing frequency, amplitude, force, and related processing parameters improves bonding quality and limits porosity.
UAM can be performed at ambient or slightly elevated temperature, potentially under an inert atmosphere.
The repair will have a mechanically consolidated, fine-grained, layered microstructure with enhanced interlayer bonding.
Real-time process verification can minimize porosity and microstructural heterogeneity in the overlay.
High-frequency ultrasonic vibrations promote solid-state bonding between successive layers.
Avoiding a liquid phase prevents the hot cracking associated with fusion-weld repair.
The UAM overlay will be uniform and defect-free and will meet or exceed the original component in tensile strength, fatigue resistance, and toughness.
The predicted properties and absence of hot cracking will persist under aggressive thermal and mechanical loading.
Traditional fusion-welding repair creates a liquid phase that leads to hot cracking and inferior repair-zone mechanical properties.
Mechanical testing and service-like thermal cycling can determine whether the repair remains within acceptable microstructural and mechanical-property limits.
The UAM process window remains uncertain for complex geometries, scale-up, reproducibility, and advanced alloy systems.
